Random Parameters Count Regression Models

Source: R/countregrp.R
countreg_rp.Rd

Random Parameters Count Regression Models

Usage

countreg_rp(
  formula,
  rpar_formula,
  data,
  family = "NB2",
  rpardists = NULL,
  dis_param_formula_1 = NULL,
  dis_param_formula_2 = NULL,
  het_mean_formula = NULL,
  het_var_formula = NULL,
  ndraws = 500,
  scrambled = FALSE,
  correlated = FALSE,
  group_var = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  method = "BFGS",
  max.iters = 1000,
  start.vals = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  stderr = "normal",
  bootstraps = NULL,
  engine = "quadrature",
  keep_data = TRUE,
  panel_id = NULL,
  mix_draws = NULL,
  weight_type = c("frequency", "sampling"),
  draws = c("per_unit", "shared"),
  cluster = NULL,
  cre = NULL,
  sp = NULL
)

Arguments

formula

an R formula. This formula should specify the outcome and the independent variables that have fixed parameters.

rpar_formula

a symbolic description of the model related specifically to the random parameters. This should not include an outcome variable. If the intercept is random, include it in this formula. If the intercept is fixed, include it in formula but not in rpar_formula.

data

a dataframe that has all of the variables in the formula and rpar_formula.

family

the name of the distribution/model type to estimate. Default is "NB2". Options include "Poisson", "NB1", "NB2", "NBP", "PIG", "Sichel", etc. (see count_families for the full list). DW, DPO, HYPERPOIS and GAMMACOUNT solve their mean equation for every observation and draw, so they are much slower here than closed-form families; consider fewer ndraws while exploring. With "GP2", the dispersion must be nonnegative: the underdispersed GP2 requires \(1 + a\mu > 0\), which random parameters with unbounded support violate for some draws of every observation. Use "GP1", whose parameter space does not depend on \(\mu\), for underdispersed random-parameter models.

rpardists

an optional named vector whose names are the random parameters and values the distribution. The distribution options include normal ("n"), lognormal ("ln"), triangular ("t"), uniform ("u"), and gamma ("g"). Values are matched to the random parameters by name; every random parameter must be named. A single unnamed value applies to all random parameters. If not provided, normal is used. See Details for how each distribution's St.Dev parameter is defined.

dis_param_formula_1

a symbolic description of the model for the first parameter of the count distribution (e.g., ln(alpha) for NB2).

dis_param_formula_2

a symbolic description of the model for the second parameter of the count distribution (if applicable).

het_mean_formula

an optional one-sided formula for heterogeneity in the means of the random parameters. Each random parameter gets its own coefficient for each variable (named HetMean:<parameter>:<variable>), and the effect is additive: \(\beta_{ik} = \mu_k + z_i'\delta_k\) (Wood and Gayah, 2025, Eq. 2). For lognormal parameters the shift is on the log scale, and for gamma parameters it is multiplicative, \(\mu_k \exp(z_i'\delta_k)\), so the mean stays positive. The intercept is dropped.

het_var_formula

an optional one-sided formula for heterogeneity in the scales of the random parameters: \(\sigma_{ik} = \sigma_k \exp(s_i'\phi)\), with \(\phi\) shared by all random parameters. The intercept is dropped.

ndraws

the number of Halton draws to use for estimating the random parameters.

scrambled

if the Halton draws should be randomized. The Halton points (each unit's own block with draws = "per_unit") are shifted by a uniform random amount per dimension, modulo 1 (a Cranley-Patterson rotation, i.e. randomized quasi-Monte Carlo), which keeps their even spread and leaves each unit's simulated likelihood unbiased. The shifts are generated from a random seed that is stored in the fit, so predictions reuse the same draws, set.seed() before fitting makes the fit reproducible, and different seeds give different draws. Earlier fits (model$draw_version below 4) used randtoolbox's scrambled ("mixed") Halton sequence, whose consecutive per-unit blocks biased the simulated log-likelihood; their predictions still use those draws.

correlated

if the random parameters should be correlated. If TRUE, only normal distributions are used.

group_var

an optional variable name (string), or a vector with one value per row, defining the panel structure (repeated measures). If provided, each panel shares one draw of the random parameters, and the likelihood and standard errors account for the panel structure.

weights

the name of a variable, or a numeric vector, of weights (see weight_type). With group_var, weights apply to whole panels (the panel log-likelihood is weighted), so they should be constant within a panel.

offset

the name of a variable, or vector of variable names, to be used as an offset (summed when several are given). An offset can instead be given with offset() in formula; use only one of the two.

method

optimization method passed to maxLik: "BFGS" (default), "NR", "BHHH", "BFGSR", "CG", "NM" or "SANN". BFGS uses the analytic gradient and is the most reliable choice. BHHH is often faster on simple models, but on harder ones it can crawl, or stop where the log-likelihood has stopped changing well short of the maximum; such stops are flagged (see Details). NR is reliable near the maximum but slow, because it differentiates the gradient numerically for its Hessian.

max.iters

maximum number of iterations.

start.vals

optional vector of starting values, one per parameter. Named values are matched to the parameters by name.

verbose

logical.

stderr

the type of standard errors: "normal" (Hessian-based, the default), "robust" (sandwich; clustered by panel when group_var is given), or "boot" (bootstrap that resamples whole panels and refits the model), or "cluster" (cluster-robust, with cluster; clusters must contain whole panels, so they may be coarser than the panels, e.g. sites within corridors).

bootstraps

the number of bootstrap samples when stderr = "boot" (default 200).

engine

the numerical method for the mixed Poisson families PLN, PGE, PW and PLL: "quadrature" (default; adaptive quadrature on the log scale, accurate for every count), "halton" (the average over Halton draws used by flexCountReg 0.1.2 and earlier, kept to reproduce earlier fits; it is badly biased for counts far in the tail) or, for PLN only, "poilog" (the poilog package).

keep_data

logical; if FALSE, the training data are not stored in the fitted object. predict() then needs newdata.

panel_id

deprecated; use group_var.

mix_draws

with engine = "halton", the number of Halton draws for integrating over the mixing distribution of the PLN, PGE, PLL and PW families (inside each random-parameter draw). The default is min(ndraws, 200). Not used by the default engine = "quadrature", which integrates adaptively.

weight_type

"frequency" (default): each weight is the number of independent observations a row stands for, so the log-likelihood, LR tests, AIC and BIC are those of the expanded data. "sampling": survey or inverse-probability weights, which only set how much each unit counts. The weighted log-likelihood is then a pseudo-likelihood: standard errors default to the robust sandwich with meat sum((w s)(w s)') and the small-sample factor G / (G - 1) for G units, so they do not change when all weights are rescaled; the number of units is the number of panels (rows without group_var) with a positive weight; bootstrap standard errors are not available; and LR tests, AIC and BIC are not valid (they are reported, with a note, by summary() and are refused by regCompTest()).

draws

"per_unit" (default): each unit (panel, or row when there is no group_var) has its own ndraws draws, a consecutive block of one Halton sequence after its first 10 points (Train 2009, Sec. 9.3.3), so the simulation errors of different units are independent. "shared": the same draws for every unit, as in earlier versions. Empirical Bayes predictions (method = "Individual") regenerate each estimation unit's own draws, matched by panel id (by row position without panels); units not in the estimation data get new draws.

cluster

clustering variable(s) for stderr = "cluster": a one-sided formula of columns of data (~ corridor; two or more, ~ corridor + year, give multiway clustering), their names, or a vector with one cluster id per row of data. Given without stderr, it sets stderr = "cluster". See vcov.flexCountReg, which also gives cluster-robust covariances after the fit.

cre

optional one-sided formula of time-varying regressors, e.g. ~ x1 + x2, for correlated random effects (Mundlak 1978): the group means of these variables (columns mean_x1, ...) are added to the mean model, so the random effect may depend on the regressors through their means. The means are computed on the estimation rows and stored with the fit: predictions for a group in the estimation data use its training means, and a new group uses the means of its own rows in newdata. cre_test() tests random against fixed effects.

sp

optional fixed smoothing parameters, one per penalty of the smooth terms (in the order of model$smooth_table); by default they are selected automatically.

Value

An object of class flexCountReg which is a list with the following components:

  • model: the fitted model object.

  • data: the data frame used to fit the model.

  • call: the matched call.

  • formula: the formula used to fit the model.

Details

Smooth terms. The formulas accept the penalized smooths of the mgcv package (s(), te(), ti(), t2()), for example y ~ s(lnaadt) + speed50, or dis_param_formula_1 = ~ s(lnlength) for a dispersion that varies smoothly. The model is then fitted by penalized maximum likelihood, with the smoothing parameters selected by generalized Fellner-Schall updates (Wood and Fasiolo 2017), which approximately maximize the restricted marginal likelihood; sp fixes them instead. Standard errors are Bayesian (\((H + S_\lambda)^{-1}\)) by default, and robust or cluster-robust ones are available. summary() reports each smooth by its effective degrees of freedom with an approximate test, the log-likelihood's degrees of freedom are the total effective degrees of freedom, and smooth_estimates() and plot_smooths() show the estimated functions. With fixed smoothing parameters the estimates equal those of mgcv::gam(); the selected smoothing parameters are close to mgcv's REML choice. Smooth terms need the mgcv package, and bootstrap standard errors are not yet available with them. In countreg_rp() smooths may enter formula, het_mean_formula, het_var_formula and the distribution-parameter formulas, but not rpar_formula: a random parameter is a coefficient that varies across units with an unknown distribution, a smooth is a function of an observed variable, and a smooth heterogeneity-in-means term lets a random parameter's mean vary smoothly with a unit attribute.

countreg.rp() is the former name of countreg_rp(). It is deprecated (a name with a dot is easily mistaken for an S3 method): it still works, with a once-per-session warning, and calls countreg_rp().

Random parameter distributions. Each random parameter is \(\beta = \mu + \sigma \upsilon\), where the :Mean and :St.Dev estimates are \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\):

  • normal ("n"): \(\upsilon \sim N(0, 1)\), so \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation.

  • uniform ("u") and triangular ("t"): \(\upsilon\) is uniform or symmetric triangular on \([-1, 1]\), so \(\beta\) lies in \([\mu - \sigma, \mu + \sigma]\). Here \(\sigma\) is a half-width; the standard deviation is \(\sigma/\sqrt{3}\) (uniform) or \(\sigma/\sqrt{6}\) (triangular). Models fitted with version 0.1.1 or earlier used \([\mu - \sigma/2, \mu + \sigma/2]\) for the uniform; their \(\sigma\) is converted automatically in predict().

  • lognormal ("ln"): \(\beta = \exp(\mu + \sigma \upsilon)\), always positive. The expected value of \(\exp(x\beta)\) is infinite for \(x > 0\), so marginal (Exact or Simulated) predictions do not exist for observations with a positive value of a lognormal random parameter's variable. Use the variable's negative (so \(x \le 0\)), a gamma random parameter, or method = "Individual" predictions instead.

  • gamma ("g"): mean \(\mu > 0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), so the coefficient is always positive.

The mixing distribution of the PLN, PGE, PLL and PW families uses its own Halton dimension, independent of the random parameters' draws.

Gradient. The optimizer uses the analytic gradient of the simulated log-likelihood: each panel's score is the average, over draws weighted by their posterior probabilities, of the family's score in the log mean times the derivative of the log mean in each parameter. The Poisson, NB1, NB2 and NBP families have closed-form scores; the other families use central differences in the log mean and in each distribution parameter, two density evaluations per parameter of the distribution whatever the number of regression parameters. A numeric gradient needs two likelihood evaluations per parameter, so fits are several times faster. options(flexCountReg.rp_gradient = "numeric") restores the numeric gradient, to check a fit.

Convergence. BHHH, NR and BFGSR stop when the log-likelihood changes by less than a tolerance between iterations, which a slow optimizer can also meet far from the maximum. After the fit, countreg_rp() computes the Newton decrement \(g'(-H)^{-1}g\) at the estimates (twice the further gain a Newton step predicts; stored as model$newton_decrement). Above 0.1, the fit is marked as not converged, with a warning.

References

Train, K. (2009). Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.

Wood, J.S., Gayah, V. (2025). Out-of-sample prediction and interpretation for random parameter generalized linear models. Accident Analysis and Prevention, 220, 108147.

Examples

# \donttest{
# Load data
data("washington_roads")
washington_roads$AADT10kplus <- ifelse(washington_roads$AADT > 10000, 1, 0)

# 1. Basic Random Parameters Negative Binomial (NB2)
rp_nb2 <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength,
                      rpar_formula = ~ -1 + speed50,
                      data = washington_roads,
                      family = "NB2",
                      rpardists = c(speed50 = "n"),
                      ndraws = 100)
summary(rp_nb2)
#> Call:
#> countreg_rp(formula = Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + lnlength, rpar_formula = ~-1 + 
#>     speed50, data = washington_roads, family = "NB2", rpardists = c(speed50 = "n"), 
#>     ndraws = 100)
#> 
#> Model: countreg_rp | family: NB2 | optimizer: BFGS
#> Iterations: 41 
#> Convergence: successful convergence 
#> 
#> Coefficients (standard errors: Hessian-based):
#>                Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)      -8.760      0.442  -19.82  < 2e-16 ***
#> lnaadt            1.080      0.052   20.79  < 2e-16 ***
#> lnlength          0.756      0.069   10.95  < 2e-16 ***
#> speed50:Mean     -0.745      0.167   -4.47  7.7e-06 ***
#> speed50:St.Dev    0.640      0.201    3.18   0.0015 ** 
#> ln(alpha)        -1.297      0.316   -4.10  4.1e-05 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -1083.165 | AIC: 2178.33 | BIC: 2210.213 
#> N: 1501

# 2. Random Parameters with Panel Structure (if 'site_id' exists)
# rp_panel <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ -1 + lnaadt,
#                        rpar_formula = ~ speed50,
#                        data = washington_roads,
#                        group_var = "site_id",
#                        family = "NB2",
#                        ndraws = 100)

# 3. Generalized Random Parameters Model with Heterogeneity
rp_gen <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt,
                      rpar_formula = ~ -1 + speed50,
                      dis_param_formula_1 = ~ lnlength, 
                      het_mean_formula = ~ AADT10kplus,
                      data = washington_roads,
                      family = "NB2",
                      rpardists = c(speed50 = "n"),
                      ndraws = 100)
summary(rp_gen)
#> Call:
#> countreg_rp(formula = Total_crashes ~ lnaadt, rpar_formula = ~-1 + 
#>     speed50, data = washington_roads, family = "NB2", rpardists = c(speed50 = "n"), 
#>     dis_param_formula_1 = ~lnlength, het_mean_formula = ~AADT10kplus, 
#>     ndraws = 100)

#> lnaadt                        0.9575     0.0531   18.04  < 2e-16 ***
#> speed50:Mean                 -0.8133     0.1894   -4.29  1.8e-05 ***
#> speed50:St.Dev                0.7099     0.2279    3.12   0.0018 ** 
#> HetMean:speed50:AADT10kplus   1.5787     0.6084    2.60   0.0095 ** 
#> ln(alpha):(Intercept)        -1.2101     0.5325   -2.27   0.0231 *

#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -1139.169 | AIC: 2292.337 | BIC: 2329.534 
#> N: 1501

# 4. Random Parameters Poisson Model with panel specification
rp_poisson <- countreg_rp(Total_crashes ~ lnaadt,
                      rpar_formula = ~ -1 + speed50,
                      het_mean_formula = ~ AADT10kplus,
                      data = washington_roads,
                      family = "POISSON",
                      rpardists = c(speed50 = "n"),
                      ndraws = 100,
                      group_var = "ID")
summary(rp_poisson)
